misconceptions.description: Misses an object or counts one twice when counting, so the count is one out.
Does not see that the last number said when counting is how many there are; counts again or gives the whole counting sequence.
Mixes up the number before and the number after, or one more and one less.
Does not cross a tens boundary correctly when counting, e.g. 28, 29, 20 or 39, 40, 50.
Thinks a group that is spread out, or takes up more space, has more objects.
Confuses teen numbers with multiples of ten or reverses their digits, e.g. 14 with 40 or 41.
Thinks only numerals can show an amount, not marks, pictures, fingers or objects.
Thinks a different arrangement of the same objects is a different number.
Adds the whole and a part instead of finding the missing part.
Counts on or back in ones instead of in the step asked for (2s, 5s, 10s and so on).
Changes the wrong digit when finding one more, ten more and so on, e.g. one more than 34 is 44.
Counts the marks on a number line instead of the jumps between them, so is one out, or ignores the scale.
Gives a digit's face value instead of its value from its place, e.g. says the 4 in 47 is worth 4.
Writes the digits in the wrong order, e.g. 3 tens and 5 ones as 53.
Reads or writes < and > the wrong way round.
Compares numbers by their ones digits, or by the number of digits shown, rather than from the largest place.
Writes numbers as they are said, e.g. sixty-three as 603 or one hundred and five as 1005.
Gives a digit the value of the place next to its own, e.g. says the 3 in 4372 is worth 3000 or 30.
Leaves out zero as a placeholder, e.g. writes 3 hundreds and 5 ones as 35.
Compares the first digits without checking how many digits each number has, e.g. thinks 9856 is greater than 10 002.
Rounds down whatever the next digit is, or simply cuts off the digits.
Rounds a number exactly halfway down instead of up, e.g. rounds 250 to 200.
Rounds to the wrong place, e.g. to the nearest 10 when asked for the nearest 100.
Counts back through zero as 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, or drops the minus sign.
Thinks a negative number with a bigger digit is greater, e.g. that −8 is greater than −3.
Adds every Roman numeral, so reads IV as 6 or XC as 110, instead of subtracting a smaller numeral before a larger one.
Uses 360° as the total for angles on a straight line, confusing it with angles at a point.
Uses 180° as the total for angles at a point, confusing it with angles on a straight line.
Adds the known angles together instead of subtracting them from the total.
Uses 360° as the total for the angles in a triangle.
Uses 180° as the total for the angles in a quadrilateral.
Thinks vertically opposite angles add up to 180° instead of being equal.
Judges the size of an angle by the length of its arms rather than the amount of turn.
Mixes up the names of angle types, for example calling an obtuse angle reflex or a reflex angle obtuse.
Names an angle with the vertex letter first or last instead of in the middle, so ∠ABC is read as the angle at A.
Reads the wrong scale of a protractor, giving 180° minus the angle.
Divides by the scale factor instead of multiplying when turning a scale drawing into real lengths (or the reverse).
Confuses clockwise with anticlockwise.
Confuses quarter, half and three-quarter turns, for example calling two right angles a quarter turn.
Mixes up parallel and perpendicular lines.
Thinks two lines are parallel just because they do not meet in the part that is drawn.
Thinks alternate or corresponding angles add up to 180° instead of being equal.
Thinks co-interior angles are equal instead of adding up to 180°.
Thinks opposite angles of a parallelogram add up to 180° instead of being equal.
Finds the total of a kite's two equal angles but forgets to share it between them.
Thinks a shape changes when it is turned, for example that a square standing on a corner is not a square.
Does not see that one shape can be a special case of another, for example that a square is a rectangle.
Counts the corners (vertices) of a shape when asked for its sides, or the reverse, or counts one side twice.
Takes the angle between the two equal sides of an isosceles triangle to be equal to the base angles.
Thinks the diagonals of a rectangle or parallelogram are lines of symmetry.
Slides half of a shape across the mirror line instead of reflecting it.
Gives the distance from a point to the mirror line when asked how far the point is from its reflection, which is twice as far.
Thinks a polygon is regular just because its sides are equal, ignoring its angles.
Uses n × 180° for the sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
Confuses the interior and exterior angles of a polygon.
Thinks the diagonals of every rectangle meet at right angles, as they do in a square.
Thinks the diagonal of a rectangle cuts its corner angle in half, as it does in a square.
Finds a missing side from a rectangle's perimeter without allowing for there being two of each side, for example subtracting one length from the whole perimeter.
Confuses the radius and the diameter, for example halving when it should double.
Mixes up a sector (between two radii) and a segment (between a chord and an arc).
Thinks every chord is a diameter, or that a diameter is not a chord.
Halves instead of doubling: thinks the angle at the centre is half the angle at the circumference.
Forgets that a tangent meets the radius at a right angle.
Thinks opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal instead of adding up to 180°.
Thinks three equal angles (AAA) prove two triangles are congruent, when they only prove the triangles are similar.
Thinks two sides and an angle that is not between them (SSA) always prove two triangles are congruent.
Labels the side next to an angle with that angle's letter, instead of the side opposite it.
Thinks any three lengths make a triangle, without checking the two shorter sides add up to more than the longest.
Measures a bearing anticlockwise from north instead of clockwise.
Gives the same bearing for the return journey instead of adding or subtracting 180°.
Gives a correct number but the wrong reason, or a reason that does not justify the step.
